items.question: What is the wavelength of a transverse wave?
items.expectedAnswer: The distance of one complete wave, e.g. crest to crest.
items.explanation: One wavelength is one full wave — measured crest-to-crest or trough-to-trough.
options: The distance of one complete wave, e.g. crest to crest.
The distance from a crest to the next trough.
The height of a crest above the rest position.

items.question: What is the frequency of a wave?
items.expectedAnswer: The number of complete waves passing a point per second.
items.explanation: Frequency is waves per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
options: The time for one complete wave.
The number of complete waves passing a point per second.

items.question: What is the period of a wave?
items.expectedAnswer: The time taken for one complete wave to pass a point.
items.explanation: Period T is the time for one full wave, measured in seconds.
options: The number of waves per second.
The time taken for one complete wave to pass a point.

items.question: Which equation links period and frequency?
items.explanation: Period and frequency are reciprocals: T = 1/f.

items.question: Which equation gives the speed of a wave?
items.explanation: Wave speed = frequency × wavelength: v = fλ.

items.question: A wave has a frequency of 5 Hz. What is its period?
A wave has a period of 0.25 s. What is its frequency?
A wave has frequency 2 Hz and wavelength 3 m. What is its speed?
Does increasing the amplitude of a wave change its wave speed (on the same medium)?
items.expectedAnswer: No — amplitude does not affect wave speed.
items.explanation: Wave speed depends on the medium, not the amplitude.
options: Yes — bigger amplitude means faster waves.
Yes — bigger amplitude means slower waves.
No — amplitude does not affect wave speed.

items.question: On a transverse wave, what is the amplitude?
items.expectedAnswer: The maximum displacement from the rest position (crest height).
items.explanation: Amplitude is the greatest displacement from rest, e.g. the height of a crest.
options: The maximum displacement from the rest position (crest height).
The number of crests per second.

items.question: A wave travels at 12 m·s⁻¹ with a wavelength of 4 m. What is its frequency?
items.explanation: v = fλ ⇒ f = v/λ = 12/4 = 3 Hz.

items.question: A wave has a speed of 20 m·s⁻¹ and a frequency of 5 Hz. What is its wavelength?
A wave has a period of 0.5 s and a wavelength of 6 m. What is its speed?
A water wave makes 10 complete waves pass a point in 5 s. What is its frequency?
items.explanation: f = number of waves/time = 10/5 = 2 Hz.

items.question: A wave of frequency 4 Hz travels at 8 m·s⁻¹. How far does one wave (one wavelength) stretch?
If the frequency of a wave doubles while the wave speed stays the same, what happens to its wavelength?
items.explanation: From v = fλ at constant v, f and λ are inversely related: double f ⇒ half λ.

items.question: The distance from one crest to the next crest of a wave is 0.5 m, and 6 waves pass each second. What is the wave speed?
A wave has period 0.1 s. How many complete waves pass a point in 2 s?
items.explanation: f = 1/T = 10 Hz; in 2 s the number of waves = f × t = 10 × 2 = 20.

items.question: Two waves travel on the same rope. Wave X has a longer wavelength than wave Y but the same speed. Which has the higher frequency?
items.explanation: At the same speed, v = fλ means shorter λ ⇒ higher f, so wave Y has the higher frequency.

items.question: A transverse wave on a string has a crest-to-trough vertical distance of 8 cm. What is its amplitude?
items.explanation: Crest-to-trough = twice the amplitude, so amplitude = 8/2 = 4 cm.

L4.T1.A1.skill_title: Describe longitudinal waves and apply v = fλ

items.question: In a longitudinal wave, how do the particles of the medium move relative to the wave's direction of travel?
items.expectedAnswer: Parallel (back and forth along) the direction of travel.
items.explanation: In a longitudinal wave particles vibrate parallel to the direction the wave travels.
options: Parallel (back and forth along) the direction of travel.
Perpendicular to the direction of travel.
They do not move at all.

items.question: What is a compression in a longitudinal wave?
items.expectedAnswer: A region where the particles are bunched closely together (high pressure).
items.explanation: A compression is a high-pressure region of closely packed particles.
options: A region where particles are spread far apart.
A region where the particles are bunched closely together (high pressure).
The highest point of the wave.

items.question: What is a rarefaction in a longitudinal wave?
items.expectedAnswer: A region where the particles are spread far apart (low pressure).
items.explanation: A rarefaction is a low-pressure region where particles are spread out.
options: A region where particles are bunched together.
The lowest point of the wave.
A region where the particles are spread far apart (low pressure).

items.question: Sound is an example of which type of wave?
items.explanation: Sound travels as a longitudinal wave (compressions and rarefactions).

items.question: How is one wavelength of a longitudinal wave measured?
items.expectedAnswer: From one compression to the next compression.
items.explanation: One wavelength = compression-to-compression (or rarefaction-to-rarefaction).
options: From a compression to the next rarefaction.
From one compression to the next compression.
From the start of the wave to its source.

items.question: Does the equation v = fλ apply to longitudinal waves?
items.expectedAnswer: Yes — it applies to all waves, including longitudinal ones.
items.explanation: v = fλ holds for every kind of wave, transverse or longitudinal.
options: Yes — it applies to all waves, including longitudinal ones.

items.question: A sound wave has a frequency of 200 Hz and a wavelength of 1.7 m. What is its speed?
A longitudinal wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 6 m. What is its speed?
Which of these is the main difference between a transverse and a longitudinal wave?
items.expectedAnswer: The direction the particles vibrate relative to the wave's travel.
items.explanation: The key difference is particle motion: perpendicular (transverse) vs parallel (longitudinal).
options: The direction the particles vibrate relative to the wave's travel.

items.question: A spring is pushed and pulled along its length, sending pulses along it. What type of wave is this?
items.explanation: Pushing/pulling along the spring's length makes compressions and rarefactions — a longitudinal wave.

items.question: A sound wave travels at 340 m·s⁻¹ with a frequency of 170 Hz. What is its wavelength?
A longitudinal wave travels at 330 m·s⁻¹ with a wavelength of 0.5 m. What is its frequency?
A sound has a period of 0.002 s and travels at 340 m·s⁻¹. What is its wavelength?
Why can sound NOT travel through a vacuum?
items.expectedAnswer: There are no particles to compress and rarefy.
items.explanation: Sound is a mechanical (longitudinal) wave that needs a medium of particles; a vacuum has none.
options: There are no particles to compress and rarefy.

items.question: In a longitudinal wave the distance between three successive compressions is 8 m. What is the wavelength?
items.explanation: Three successive compressions span two wavelengths, so λ = 8/2 = 4 m.

items.question: A loudspeaker vibrates at 256 Hz, producing sound that travels at 340 m·s⁻¹. What is the wavelength?
Which statement about energy in a longitudinal wave is correct?
items.expectedAnswer: The wave transfers energy through the medium without transporting the particles along.
items.explanation: Particles only vibrate about fixed positions; the energy moves through the medium, not the particles themselves.
options: The particles travel along with the wave from source to receiver.
The wave transfers energy through the medium without transporting the particles along.

items.question: If the frequency of a sound increases while the speed of sound stays the same, what happens to its wavelength?
items.explanation: At constant v, v = fλ means higher f gives shorter λ.

items.question: A bat emits a sound of wavelength 0.008 m that travels at 340 m·s⁻¹. What is its frequency?
items.explanation: f = v/λ = 340/0.008 = 42 500 Hz (ultrasound).

items.question: Both a transverse water wave and a longitudinal sound wave have frequency 100 Hz. What does this tell you?
items.expectedAnswer: Each produces 100 complete waves per second, regardless of type.
items.explanation: Frequency means waves per second for any wave type; both make 100 per second.
options: The water wave is faster because it is transverse.
Each produces 100 complete waves per second, regardless of type.
Frequency only applies to transverse waves.

L4.T1.A2.skill_title: Relate properties of sound to pitch, loudness and quality

items.question: Which property of a sound wave determines its pitch?
items.explanation: Pitch is set by frequency: higher frequency = higher pitch.

items.question: Which property of a sound wave determines its loudness?
items.explanation: Loudness is set by amplitude: bigger amplitude = louder sound.

items.question: A singer sings a higher note. What has happened to the sound wave?
items.explanation: A higher note means higher pitch, which means a higher frequency.

items.question: Turning up the volume on a speaker (same note) changes which wave property?
items.explanation: A louder sound at the same pitch has a larger amplitude (same frequency).

items.question: In which medium does sound travel fastest?
items.explanation: Sound is fastest in solids (particles close together) and cannot travel in a vacuum.

items.question: What is ultrasound?
items.expectedAnswer: Sound with a frequency above the human hearing range (above 20 000 Hz).
items.explanation: Ultrasound has a frequency higher than 20 000 Hz, above what humans can hear.
options: Sound that travels through a vacuum.
Sound with a frequency above the human hearing range (above 20 000 Hz).

items.question: What causes an echo?
items.expectedAnswer: Sound reflecting off a hard surface and returning to the listener.
items.explanation: An echo is reflected sound bouncing back from a surface.
options: Sound reflecting off a hard surface and returning to the listener.

items.question: Two sounds have the same pitch and loudness but come from a guitar and a flute and still sound different. Which property differs?
items.explanation: Quality (timbre) depends on the waveform shape, letting us tell instruments apart.

items.question: Can sound travel through outer space (a vacuum)?
items.expectedAnswer: No — sound needs a medium of particles.
items.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave; with no particles in a vacuum it cannot travel.
options: Yes — but only if it is loud enough.
No — sound needs a medium of particles.

items.question: A drummer hits a drum harder. How does the sound change?
items.explanation: Hitting harder gives the wave more amplitude, making it louder; pitch (frequency) is unchanged.

items.question: Sound travels at about 340 m·s⁻¹ in air. A person shouts at a cliff and hears the echo 2 s later. How far away is the cliff?
items.explanation: The sound travels to the cliff and back in 2 s, so total distance = 340 × 2 = 680 m; the cliff is half of that = 340 m.

items.question: A sonar pulse from a ship returns from the seabed after 0.4 s. If sound travels at 1500 m·s⁻¹ in water, how deep is the seabed?
items.explanation: Total distance = 1500 × 0.4 = 600 m (down and back). Depth = 600/2 = 300 m.

items.question: Why does a high-pitched whistle have a shorter wavelength than a low-pitched hum in the same air?
items.expectedAnswer: Higher frequency at the same speed gives a shorter wavelength (v = fλ).
items.explanation: At fixed speed, v = fλ means higher f ⇒ shorter λ.
options: Higher frequency at the same speed gives a shorter wavelength (v = fλ).
Higher pitch has a larger amplitude.

items.question: Which change would make a sound BOTH higher pitched and quieter?
items.expectedAnswer: Increase the frequency and decrease the amplitude.
items.explanation: Higher pitch = higher frequency; quieter = smaller amplitude.
options: Increase the frequency and decrease the amplitude.
Decrease the frequency and increase the amplitude.

items.question: A sound of frequency 680 Hz travels at 340 m·s⁻¹ in air. What is its wavelength?
An ultrasound scanner uses 2 000 000 Hz waves at 1500 m·s⁻¹ in tissue. What is the wavelength?
items.explanation: λ = v/f = 1500/2 000 000 = 0.00075 m (0.75 mm) — short wavelengths give detailed images.

items.question: Why is the speed of sound greater in water than in air?
items.expectedAnswer: Particles in water are closer together, so vibrations pass on faster.
items.explanation: Sound travels faster where particles are closer (liquids and solids) than in gases.
options: Particles in water are closer together, so vibrations pass on faster.

items.question: Two notes are played. Note P has double the frequency of note Q. How do they sound?
items.expectedAnswer: Note P has a higher pitch than note Q.
items.explanation: Double the frequency means a higher pitch; frequency does not change loudness or speed.
options: Note P is louder than note Q.
Note P travels faster than note Q.
Note P has a higher pitch than note Q.

items.question: A bat uses echolocation, sending out a pulse that returns after 0.01 s. If sound travels at 340 m·s⁻¹, how far away is the object?
items.explanation: Total path = 340 × 0.01 = 3.4 m (there and back); object distance = 3.4/2 = 1.7 m.

items.question: On an oscilloscope two sound waves have the same height but one is more tightly packed (more waves across the screen). What differs?
items.expectedAnswer: The tightly packed wave has a higher frequency (higher pitch).
items.explanation: Same height = same amplitude (loudness); more waves across = higher frequency (pitch).
options: The tightly packed wave is louder.
The tightly packed wave has a higher frequency (higher pitch).
The tightly packed wave has a larger amplitude.

L5.T1.A1.skill_title: Describe the EM spectrum and relate frequency, wavelength and energy

items.question: What do all electromagnetic waves have in common in a vacuum?
items.expectedAnswer: They all travel at the speed of light, c = 3×10⁸ m·s⁻¹.
items.explanation: Every EM wave travels at c = 3×10⁸ m·s⁻¹ in a vacuum, regardless of band.
options: They all travel at the speed of light, c = 3×10⁸ m·s⁻¹.
They all have the same frequency.
They all have the same wavelength.

items.question: Which equation relates the speed, frequency and wavelength of an EM wave?
items.explanation: For EM waves c = fλ, where c is the speed of light.

items.question: Which equation gives the energy of a photon of EM radiation?
items.explanation: Photon energy E = hf, where h is Planck's constant.

items.question: Which band of the EM spectrum has the HIGHEST frequency and energy?
items.explanation: Gamma rays have the highest frequency, shortest wavelength and most energy.

items.question: Which band of the EM spectrum has the LOWEST frequency and energy?
items.explanation: Radio waves have the lowest frequency and least energy of the EM spectrum.

items.question: As frequency increases across the EM spectrum, what happens to the wavelength?
items.explanation: Since c = fλ at constant c, higher frequency means shorter wavelength.

items.question: As frequency increases across the EM spectrum, what happens to the photon energy?
items.explanation: E = hf, so higher frequency means higher photon energy.

items.question: Which type of EM radiation is used for communication, such as broadcasting and cellphones?
items.explanation: Radio waves and microwaves are used for broadcasting and mobile communication.

items.question: Which EM radiation is used in medical imaging to see broken bones?
items.explanation: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone, so they image fractures.

items.question: Visible light, infrared and ultraviolet are all examples of...
items.explanation: These are all bands of the electromagnetic spectrum (transverse EM waves).

items.question: Place these in order of INCREASING frequency: ultraviolet, radio, visible light.
items.explanation: Increasing frequency: radio (low) → visible → ultraviolet (higher).

items.question: An EM wave has a frequency of 6×10¹⁴ Hz. What is its wavelength? (c = 3×10⁸ m·s⁻¹)
items.explanation: λ = c/f = 3×10⁸ / 6×10¹⁴ = 5×10⁻⁷ m (visible light).

items.question: A radio wave has a wavelength of 3 m. What is its frequency? (c = 3×10⁸ m·s⁻¹)
Which statement comparing gamma rays and radio waves is correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Gamma rays have higher frequency, shorter wavelength and more energy than radio waves.
items.explanation: Gamma: high f, short λ, high E. Radio: low f, long λ, low E. Both travel at c.
options: Radio waves have more energy than gamma rays.
Gamma rays have higher frequency, shorter wavelength and more energy than radio waves.
They have the same frequency but different speeds.

items.question: Why are gamma rays more dangerous to living tissue than radio waves?
items.expectedAnswer: They have much higher photon energy and can ionise atoms.
items.explanation: High-frequency gamma photons carry enough energy (E = hf) to ionise and damage cells.
options: They travel much faster than radio waves.
They have much higher photon energy and can ionise atoms.

items.question: Calculate the energy of a photon of frequency 5×10¹⁴ Hz. (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J·s)
Two EM waves travel in a vacuum: an X-ray and a microwave. Which travels faster?
items.expectedAnswer: They travel at the same speed (c).
items.explanation: All EM waves travel at c = 3×10⁸ m·s⁻¹ in a vacuum, regardless of band.
options: The X-ray, because it has more energy.
They travel at the same speed (c).
The microwave, because it has a longer wavelength.

items.question: Infrared radiation is mainly associated with which effect?
items.expectedAnswer: Heating — it is felt as warmth.
items.explanation: Infrared is thermal radiation, felt as heat; it is used in heaters and remote controls.
options: Heating — it is felt as warmth.

items.question: An EM wave has a wavelength of 1×10⁻¹⁰ m. Using the spectrum order, which band is it most likely in? (c = 3×10⁸ m·s⁻¹)
items.explanation: A 10⁻¹⁰ m wavelength is extremely short, placing it in the X-ray/gamma region.

items.question: Why does the dual nature of EM radiation mean it can behave as both a wave and a particle?
items.expectedAnswer: It shows wave properties (like diffraction) and particle properties (photons with energy hf).
items.explanation: EM radiation has a dual nature: wave-like (interference, diffraction) and particle-like (photons of energy E = hf).
options: It is sometimes a sound wave and sometimes light.
It shows wave properties (like diffraction) and particle properties (photons with energy hf).
It changes speed between the two behaviours.

L6.T1.A1.skill_title: Describe magnetic fields, poles and the Earth's magnetic field

items.question: What happens when the north pole of one magnet is brought near the north pole of another?
items.explanation: Like poles repel; two north poles push apart.

items.question: What happens when the north pole of one magnet is brought near the south pole of another?
items.explanation: Unlike poles (north–south) attract.

items.question: Outside a bar magnet, in which direction do the magnetic field lines point?
items.expectedAnswer: From the north pole to the south pole.
items.explanation: By convention, field lines run from N to S outside the magnet.
options: From the south pole to the north pole.
From the north pole to the south pole.

items.question: Can two magnetic field lines ever cross each other?
items.explanation: Magnetic field lines never cross; a crossing would mean two field directions at one point.
options: Yes — they cross at the poles.
Yes — they cross midway between magnets.

items.question: Where is a bar magnet's magnetic field strongest?
items.expectedAnswer: At the poles, where the field lines are closest together.
items.explanation: Closely spaced field lines at the poles indicate the strongest field.
options: In the middle of the magnet.
At the poles, where the field lines are closest together.
It is the same strength everywhere.

items.question: What does the closeness (density) of magnetic field lines show?
items.expectedAnswer: How strong the field is (closer lines = stronger field).
items.explanation: The spacing of field lines represents field strength: closer = stronger.
options: How fast the magnet is moving.
How strong the field is (closer lines = stronger field).

items.question: Why does a freely suspended bar magnet always come to rest pointing roughly north–south?
items.expectedAnswer: It lines up with the Earth's magnetic field.
items.explanation: The Earth acts like a giant magnet, so a free magnet aligns with the Earth's field (a compass).
options: It lines up with the Earth's magnetic field.
It is pulled by the Sun.
It is repelled by all metals.

items.question: A compass needle is itself a small...
items.explanation: A compass needle is a small magnet free to rotate and align with a magnetic field.

items.question: Two unlike poles are placed near each other. How are the field lines between them arranged?
items.expectedAnswer: They run directly from the north pole across to the south pole.
items.explanation: Between unlike poles the field lines link N to S directly (an attractive pattern).
options: They point away from each other.
There are no field lines between them.
They run directly from the north pole across to the south pole.

items.question: Which material is magnetic (attracted to a magnet)?
items.explanation: Iron (and steel, nickel, cobalt) is magnetic; copper and wood are not.

items.question: Inside a bar magnet, the field lines point...
items.expectedAnswer: from the south pole to the north pole (completing a loop).
items.explanation: Field lines form closed loops: N→S outside, and S→N inside the magnet.
options: from the north pole to the south pole.
from the south pole to the north pole (completing a loop).

items.question: A compass is placed near a bar magnet's north pole. Which way does the compass's north (red) end point?
items.expectedAnswer: Away from the magnet's north pole (it is repelled).
items.explanation: Like poles repel, so the compass north end points away from the magnet's north pole, along the field.
options: Away from the magnet's north pole (it is repelled).

items.question: The Earth's magnetic field behaves as if there is a bar magnet inside the Earth. Where is this imaginary magnet's SOUTH pole?
items.explanation: A compass north points geographically north because the Earth's magnetic south is near the geographic north.
options: At the centre of the Earth only.

items.question: Why does a compass needle's north end point towards the Earth's geographic north?
items.expectedAnswer: The Earth's magnetic south pole lies near the geographic north, attracting the needle's north end.
items.explanation: Unlike poles attract: the compass north is drawn to the Earth's magnetic south, located near geographic north.
options: The geographic north is also a magnetic north pole.
The Earth's magnetic south pole lies near the geographic north, attracting the needle's north end.
The needle is attracted to the cold.

items.question: Two bar magnets are placed end to end with field lines that seem to push apart and avoid each other between them. Which poles face each other?
items.expectedAnswer: Two like poles (e.g. N and N).
items.explanation: Like poles repel, producing a field pattern where lines push apart with a neutral point between.
options: A north and a south pole.
Two like poles (e.g. N and N).

items.question: What is a 'neutral point' in a magnetic field?
items.expectedAnswer: A point where the magnetic fields cancel and the net field is zero.
items.explanation: At a neutral point the fields from different sources cancel, giving zero net field.
options: A point where the magnetic fields cancel and the net field is zero.
The strongest point of the field.
The centre of a single magnet.

items.question: You have an unmarked bar magnet and a compass. How can you identify the magnet's north pole?
items.expectedAnswer: The compass end that points to the Earth's north is its north; the magnet pole that repels it is north.
items.explanation: The compass north end is repelled by the magnet's north pole (like poles repel), identifying it.
options: The pole that attracts the compass north end is north.
The compass end that points to the Earth's north is its north; the magnet pole that repels it is north.
Both poles attract the compass equally.

items.question: Iron filings sprinkled around a bar magnet line up to show...
items.expectedAnswer: the shape and direction of the magnetic field.
items.explanation: Iron filings become tiny magnets and align along the field lines, revealing the field pattern.
options: the electric current in the magnet.
the shape and direction of the magnetic field.

items.question: Which statement about magnetic poles is correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Poles always occur in north–south pairs; a single isolated pole has never been found.
items.explanation: Magnetic poles always come in pairs; cutting a magnet makes two smaller magnets, each with N and S.
options: Poles always occur in north–south pairs; a single isolated pole has never been found.
You can have a magnet with only a north pole.
Cutting a magnet in half removes one pole.

items.question: A magnet is cut in half across its middle. What are the two pieces?
items.expectedAnswer: Two complete magnets, each with its own north and south pole.
items.explanation: Each half becomes a full magnet with both poles — isolated single poles do not exist.
options: One north-only and one south-only magnet.
Two complete magnets, each with its own north and south pole.

L7.T1.A1.skill_title: Apply charge concepts: charging, conservation and quantisation

items.question: How many kinds of electric charge are there?
items.explanation: There are two kinds of charge: positive and negative.

items.question: Two objects carry like charges (both negative). What is the force between them?
items.explanation: Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

items.question: When a plastic rod is rubbed with a cloth and becomes negatively charged, what has been transferred?
items.explanation: Only electrons move; gaining electrons makes the rod negative.

items.question: An object becomes positively charged by friction. What happened to its electrons?
items.explanation: Losing electrons leaves an object with a net positive charge.

items.question: What is the principle of conservation of charge?
items.expectedAnswer: Charge is neither created nor destroyed, only transferred.
items.explanation: Total charge is conserved: it is transferred between objects, never made or lost.
options: Charge is neither created nor destroyed, only transferred.

items.question: What is the charge on a single electron?
items.explanation: An electron carries a charge of −1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C (the elementary charge).

items.question: Which equation relates charge Q to the number of electrons n?
items.explanation: Charge is quantised: Q = ne, where e is the charge on one electron.

items.question: What does it mean that charge is 'quantised'?
items.expectedAnswer: Charge comes only in whole-number multiples of the electron's charge.
items.explanation: Quantisation means Q = ne with n a whole number — charge cannot be a fraction of e.
options: Charge can take any value at all.
Charge comes only in whole-number multiples of the electron's charge.

items.question: An object has a charge of −3.2×10⁻¹⁹ C. How many excess electrons does it have?
items.explanation: n = Q/e = 3.2×10⁻¹⁹ / 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ = 2 electrons.

items.question: A neutral atom has equal numbers of...
items.explanation: Neutral means equal positive and negative charge, i.e. equal protons and electrons.

items.question: Two identical metal spheres carry charges of +6 nC and +2 nC. They are touched together and separated. What charge is on each afterwards?
items.explanation: Identical spheres share charge equally: (6 + 2)/2 = 4 nC each.

items.question: Two identical metal spheres carry charges of +8 nC and −2 nC. After touching and separating, what is the charge on each?
items.explanation: Total = +8 + (−2) = +6 nC; shared equally = +3 nC each.

items.question: How many electrons make up a charge of −1.6×10⁻¹⁸ C?
items.explanation: n = Q/e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁸ / 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ = 10 electrons.

items.question: An object gains 5×10¹² electrons. What is the magnitude of its charge?
Why does a positively charged rod attract small neutral pieces of paper?
items.expectedAnswer: It induces a charge separation in the paper, pulling the opposite charge closer.
items.explanation: The rod polarises the neutral paper; the nearer (opposite) charge is attracted more than the far charge is repelled.
options: The paper is also positively charged.
It induces a charge separation in the paper, pulling the opposite charge closer.

items.question: Sphere A (+4 nC) touches identical sphere B (0 nC). What is the charge on B after separation?
items.explanation: Total +4 nC shared equally between two identical spheres: +2 nC each.

items.question: When a rod is charged by friction, why does the cloth gain the opposite charge to the rod?
items.expectedAnswer: Electrons transferred from one to the other; one gains them, the other loses them.
items.explanation: Conservation of charge: electrons leaving the cloth land on the rod, giving them opposite charges.
options: Electrons transferred from one to the other; one gains them, the other loses them.

items.question: A charge of −4.8×10⁻¹⁹ C means the object has how many excess electrons?
items.explanation: n = 4.8×10⁻¹⁹ / 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ = 3 electrons.

items.question: Could an object have a charge of exactly −2.4×10⁻¹⁹ C?
items.expectedAnswer: No — it is not a whole-number multiple of the electron's charge.
items.explanation: Charge is quantised in multiples of 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C; −2.4×10⁻¹⁹ C (1.5 electrons) is not possible.
options: No — it is not a whole-number multiple of the electron's charge.
Yes — any charge value is allowed.

items.question: Two identical spheres, +10 nC and −4 nC, are touched together then separated, then one is touched to a third identical neutral sphere. What is the charge on that third sphere?
items.explanation: First pair: (10 − 4)/2 = +3 nC each. One (+3 nC) touches neutral: (3 + 0)/2 = +1.5 nC.

L8.T1.A1.skill_title: Define current, potential difference and EMF and measure them correctly

items.question: What is electric current?
items.expectedAnswer: The rate of flow of charge.
items.explanation: Current is the rate at which charge flows: I = Q/t.
options: The rate of flow of charge.

items.question: How is an ammeter connected in a circuit?
items.explanation: An ammeter measures current and must be connected in series so the current flows through it.

items.question: How is a voltmeter connected in a circuit?
items.explanation: A voltmeter measures potential difference and is connected in parallel across the component.

items.question: What is potential difference (voltage) across a component?
items.expectedAnswer: The energy transferred per unit charge as it passes through the component.
items.explanation: Potential difference is energy per coulomb transferred between two points.
options: The energy transferred per unit charge as it passes through the component.
The rate of flow of charge.
The total charge in the circuit.

items.question: What is the EMF of a cell?
items.expectedAnswer: The total energy supplied per unit charge by the cell.
items.explanation: EMF is the energy per coulomb provided by the source to the charges.
options: The total energy supplied per unit charge by the cell.

items.question: Which equation relates charge, current and time?
items.explanation: Charge = current × time: Q = It.

items.question: In what unit is electric current measured?
items.explanation: Current is measured in amperes (A).

items.question: A current of 2 A flows for 5 s. How much charge passes a point?
In what unit is potential difference measured?
items.explanation: Potential difference is measured in volts (V).

items.question: A charge of 12 C flows past a point in 4 s. What is the current?
An ammeter is mistakenly connected in parallel across a resistor. What is the likely problem?
items.expectedAnswer: It has very low resistance, so it short-circuits the resistor and a large current may flow.
items.explanation: Ammeters have very low resistance and must be in series; in parallel they short the component.
options: It will read the correct current.
It has very low resistance, so it short-circuits the resistor and a large current may flow.
It will read the potential difference instead.

items.question: A voltmeter is mistakenly connected in series. What is the likely problem?
items.expectedAnswer: Its very high resistance almost stops the current, so the circuit barely works.
items.explanation: Voltmeters have very high resistance and must be in parallel; in series they block the current.
options: It will read the correct voltage.
It will read the current instead.
Its very high resistance almost stops the current, so the circuit barely works.

items.question: A current of 0.5 A flows through a lamp for 2 minutes. How much charge passes through it?
items.explanation: Convert time: 2 min = 120 s. Q = It = 0.5 × 120 = 60 C.

items.question: How much charge flows when a current of 3 A is maintained for 0.5 minutes?
Why is EMF usually slightly larger than the terminal voltage of a real battery when current flows?
items.expectedAnswer: Some energy per coulomb is used inside the battery's own (internal) resistance.
items.explanation: A real cell has internal resistance, so the terminal voltage is the EMF minus the 'lost volts' inside.
options: EMF is always smaller than terminal voltage.
Terminal voltage includes the EMF twice.
Some energy per coulomb is used inside the battery's own (internal) resistance.

items.question: A battery delivers 30 J of energy to every 2 C of charge passing through it. What is its EMF?
items.explanation: EMF = energy per charge = 30/2 = 15 V (J per C).

items.question: If 24 J of energy is transferred by 4 C of charge passing through a resistor, what is the potential difference across it?
items.explanation: V = energy/charge = 24/4 = 6 V.

items.question: What does it mean physically that the current is the same everywhere in a simple series circuit?
items.expectedAnswer: Charge is not used up; the same rate of flow passes every component.
items.explanation: Charge is conserved, so the same current flows through each series component (charge is not consumed).
options: The charge is shared out and reduces along the circuit.
Charge is not used up; the same rate of flow passes every component.

items.question: A current of 5 A flows for 4 s. The same charge then flows in 2 s through another wire. What is the current in the second wire?
items.explanation: Charge Q = It = 5 × 4 = 20 C. In the second wire I = Q/t = 20/2 = 10 A.

items.question: Which instrument arrangement correctly measures both the current through and the voltage across a single resistor?
items.expectedAnswer: Ammeter in series with the resistor; voltmeter in parallel across it.
items.explanation: Current needs the ammeter in series; voltage needs the voltmeter in parallel across the resistor.
options: Ammeter in parallel; voltmeter in series.
Ammeter in series with the resistor; voltmeter in parallel across it.
Both in series with the resistor.

L8.T1.A2.skill_title: Apply current and potential difference rules in series and parallel circuits

items.question: What is resistance?
items.expectedAnswer: The opposition of a component to the flow of current.
items.explanation: Resistance opposes current flow and is defined by R = V/I.
options: The opposition of a component to the flow of current.
The rate of flow of charge.
The energy supplied by the cell.

items.question: Which equation defines resistance?
items.explanation: Resistance R = potential difference ÷ current = V/I.

items.question: In a series circuit, the current is...
items.explanation: In series there is one path, so the same current flows through all components.

items.question: In a series circuit, the potential differences across the components...
items.expectedAnswer: add up to the total supply voltage.
items.explanation: In series, the component voltages add up to the battery's EMF.
options: add up to the total supply voltage.
are the same across each component.

items.question: In a parallel circuit, the potential difference across each branch is...
items.explanation: Parallel branches all connect across the same two points, so they have the same voltage.
options: shared so each branch gets less.

items.question: In a parallel circuit, the currents in the branches...
items.expectedAnswer: add up to the total current from the source.
items.explanation: The main current splits between branches and the branch currents add up to the total.
options: are the same in each branch always.
add up to the total current from the source.

items.question: A resistor has 6 V across it and 2 A through it. What is its resistance?
Two resistors, 3 Ω and 5 Ω, are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
items.explanation: Series resistances add: 3 + 5 = 8 Ω.

items.question: A 4 V potential difference drives a current of 0.5 A through a resistor. What is the resistance?
Adding more resistors in parallel to a circuit has what effect on the total resistance?
items.explanation: More parallel paths let more current flow, so the total resistance decreases.

items.question: Two resistors, 6 Ω and 3 Ω, are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
Two equal 4 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
items.explanation: For two equal resistors in parallel, R = R/2 = 4/2 = 2 Ω.

items.question: In a series circuit, a 12 V battery is connected to two resistors. If 8 V is measured across the first, what is the voltage across the second?
items.explanation: Series voltages add to the supply: 12 − 8 = 4 V.

items.question: In a parallel circuit, the total current from the battery is 6 A. One branch carries 2.5 A. What does the other branch carry?
items.explanation: Branch currents add to the total: 6 − 2.5 = 3.5 A.

items.question: A series circuit has a 2 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor across a 12 V battery. What is the current in the circuit?
items.explanation: Total R = 2 + 4 = 6 Ω; I = V/R = 12/6 = 2 A (same throughout series).

items.question: Why does a bulb get dimmer when an extra bulb is added IN SERIES with it?
items.expectedAnswer: Total resistance rises, so the current through both bulbs drops.
items.explanation: Adding series resistance increases total R, reducing the current and so the brightness.
options: Total resistance rises, so the current through both bulbs drops.
The voltage across each bulb rises.

items.question: Two resistors, 2 Ω and 2 Ω, are in parallel, and this combination is in series with a 3 Ω resistor. What is the total resistance?
items.explanation: Parallel pair: 2 in parallel with 2 = 1 Ω. Series: 1 + 3 = 4 Ω.

items.question: In a parallel circuit, why does each branch have the same voltage as the battery?
items.expectedAnswer: Each branch is connected directly across the same two supply points.
items.explanation: Parallel branches share the same two nodes, so each has the full supply voltage across it.
options: Each branch is connected directly across the same two supply points.

items.question: A 10 V battery drives a series circuit with total resistance 5 Ω. What current flows, and how does it compare in each resistor?
items.expectedAnswer: 2 A, the same through every resistor.
items.explanation: I = V/R = 10/5 = 2 A; in series the same current flows through all components.
options: 2 A, the same through every resistor.
2 A, but split between the resistors.

items.question: Three identical lamps are connected in parallel across a battery. Compared with one lamp alone, the total current drawn from the battery is...
items.expectedAnswer: greater (more branches draw more total current).
items.explanation: Each parallel lamp draws its own current, so the total current from the battery increases.
options: greater (more branches draw more total current).

L9.T1.A1.skill_title: Classify matter as mixtures, pure substances, elements, compounds, metals and non-metals

items.question: Which of these is a pure substance?
items.explanation: Distilled water has a fixed composition (a pure compound). Sea water and air are mixtures.

items.question: Which of these is a mixture?
items.explanation: Air is a mixture of gases. Oxygen and copper are pure substances.

items.question: What is an element?
items.expectedAnswer: A pure substance made of only one kind of atom.
items.explanation: An element contains only one type of atom (e.g. oxygen, copper).
options: A substance made of two or more atoms chemically bonded.
A pure substance made of only one kind of atom.

items.question: What is a compound?
items.expectedAnswer: A pure substance of two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio.
items.explanation: A compound has different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio (e.g. water, CO₂).
options: A pure substance of two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio.
A mixture that can be separated physically.
A substance made of one kind of atom.

items.question: Which is a homogeneous mixture?
items.explanation: A salt solution is uniform throughout (homogeneous). Sand-water and oil-water are heterogeneous.

items.question: Which is a heterogeneous mixture?
items.expectedAnswer: A mixture of sand and iron filings
items.explanation: Sand and iron filings are non-uniform (heterogeneous). A sugar solution is homogeneous; nitrogen is pure.
options: A mixture of sand and iron filings

items.question: Which property is typical of a metal?
items.expectedAnswer: Good conductor of electricity and malleable.
items.explanation: Metals conduct electricity and heat well and are malleable/ductile.
options: Good conductor of electricity and malleable.
Always a gas at room temperature.

items.question: Which property is typical of a non-metal?
items.explanation: Non-metals are generally poor conductors, brittle if solid, and dull.

items.question: What is a metalloid (semi-metal)?
items.expectedAnswer: An element with properties between metals and non-metals (e.g. silicon).
items.explanation: Metalloids like silicon have intermediate properties and are used as semiconductors.
options: An element with properties between metals and non-metals (e.g. silicon).

items.question: Which material is a good electrical insulator?
items.explanation: Plastic does not conduct electricity (insulator); copper and aluminium are conductors.

items.question: A semiconductor such as silicon conducts electricity...
items.explanation: Unlike metals, a semiconductor conducts more as temperature rises.
options: not at all under any conditions.

items.question: Which substance is magnetic?
items.explanation: Iron is magnetic; copper and glass are not.

items.question: Water can be broken down by electrolysis into hydrogen and oxygen. This shows that water is...
items.explanation: Being chemically split into different elements (H and O) means water is a compound, not an element.

items.question: Brass is made of copper and zinc that can be present in varying proportions. Brass is therefore...
items.explanation: Varying proportions and no fixed chemical formula mean brass is a mixture (alloy).

items.question: A clear, colourless liquid boils over a range of temperatures rather than at one fixed point. What does this suggest?
items.expectedAnswer: It is a mixture, not a pure substance.
items.explanation: Pure substances have sharp, fixed melting/boiling points; a boiling range indicates a mixture.
options: It is a mixture, not a pure substance.

items.question: Which list contains only elements?
items.explanation: Copper, oxygen and carbon are all single-atom-type substances (elements). Water and salt are compounds; air is a mixture.

items.question: Chromatography separates the dyes in an ink. This is evidence that the ink is...
items.expectedAnswer: a mixture of different coloured substances.
items.explanation: Separating it into components by physical means shows the ink is a mixture.
options: a mixture of different coloured substances.

items.question: An element is shiny, conducts electricity, but is brittle and conducts better when warmed. It is most likely...
items.explanation: Intermediate properties (conducts but brittle, conductivity rising with temperature) point to a metalloid.

items.question: Why is copper used for electrical wiring but plastic used to coat the wires?
items.expectedAnswer: Copper is a good conductor; plastic is a good insulator.
items.explanation: Copper conducts the current; the plastic insulation prevents shocks and short circuits.
options: Copper is a good conductor; plastic is a good insulator.

items.question: Which classification is correct for carbon dioxide (CO₂)?
items.explanation: CO₂ is two elements (C and O) chemically bonded in a fixed ratio — a pure compound.

L9.T1.A2.skill_title: Write and interpret names and formulae of substances

items.question: What is the chemical formula of sodium chloride?
items.explanation: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ combine 1:1, giving NaCl.

items.question: What is the chemical formula of water?
items.explanation: Water is two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen: H₂O. (H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide.)

items.question: What is the name of the compound CO₂?
items.explanation: The prefix di- means two oxygen atoms: carbon dioxide.

items.question: The ending '-ide' (as in chloride) usually indicates...
items.expectedAnswer: a simple ion of a single element.
items.explanation: -ide is used for simple ions like chloride (Cl⁻), oxide (O²⁻), sulphide (S²⁻).
options: a simple ion of a single element.

items.question: Which ion is the sulphate ion?
items.explanation: Sulphate is SO₄²⁻; sulphite is SO₃²⁻ and sulphide is S²⁻.

items.question: What is the formula of calcium chloride? (Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻)
items.explanation: One Ca²⁺ needs two Cl⁻ to balance charge: CaCl₂.

items.question: What does the prefix 'mono-' mean in a compound name like carbon monoxide?
items.explanation: Mono- = one; carbon monoxide is CO (one oxygen).

items.question: The ending '-ate' (as in nitrate, NO₃⁻) usually indicates an ion that...
items.explanation: -ate ions (nitrate, sulphate, carbonate) contain oxygen.

items.question: What is the name of the compound with formula MgO? (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻)
items.explanation: Mg²⁺ + O²⁻ → MgO, named magnesium oxide (no prefix needed for ionic compounds).

items.question: Which formula correctly uses brackets for a polyatomic ion?
items.explanation: When a polyatomic ion is used more than once, enclose it in brackets: Ca(NO₃)₂.

items.question: What is the formula of aluminium oxide? (Al³⁺ and O²⁻)
items.explanation: Balance charges by crossing over: 2×Al³⁺ and 3×O²⁻ give Al₂O₃ (total +6 and −6).

items.question: What is the formula of sodium carbonate? (Na⁺ and CO₃²⁻)
items.explanation: Two Na⁺ balance one CO₃²⁻: Na₂CO₃.

items.question: What is the name of the compound N₂O₃?
items.explanation: Covalent naming uses prefixes for both elements: di- (2) nitrogen, tri- (3) oxide.

items.question: What is the formula of ammonium sulphate? (NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻)
items.explanation: Two NH₄⁺ balance one SO₄²⁻; the ammonium ion needs brackets: (NH₄)₂SO₄.

items.question: Which name correctly distinguishes the compound FeCl₃ from FeCl₂?
items.explanation: Transition metals can have different charges, shown with Roman numerals: Fe³⁺ = iron(III).

items.question: What is the formula of potassium nitrate? (K⁺ and NO₃⁻)
items.explanation: K⁺ and NO₃⁻ combine 1:1: KNO₃.

items.question: Why is the name 'sodium monochloride' incorrect for NaCl?
items.expectedAnswer: Prefixes like mono- are for covalent compounds, not ionic ones.
items.explanation: Ionic compounds (metal + non-metal) are named without prefixes: sodium chloride.
options: Prefixes like mono- are for covalent compounds, not ionic ones.

items.question: What is the formula of magnesium nitrate? (Mg²⁺ and NO₃⁻)
items.explanation: One Mg²⁺ needs two NO₃⁻; brackets are needed: Mg(NO₃)₂.

items.question: Which compound is named correctly?
items.explanation: CaCO₃ contains the carbonate ion (CO₃²⁻), so it is calcium carbonate.

items.question: What is the formula of iron(II) sulphate? (Fe²⁺ and SO₄²⁻)
items.explanation: Fe²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ both have charge 2, so they combine 1:1: FeSO₄.
